newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Main parties in Pakistan's general election.
newsitem.headline: Main parties in Pakistan's general election.

text.p: Fourteen main parties are contesting Monday's national and provincial assembly elections in Pakistan.
The following is a brief profile of the parties:

-- Pakistan People's Party (PPP) was founded by Zulfikar Ali Bhutto in 1967 and is now led by his daughter Benazir, who was sacked for a second time as prime minister on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule. The PPP has its main strongholds in the southern province of Sindh.

-- Pakistan Muslim League (PML) was founded by the father of Pakistan, Mohammad Ali Jinnah and is now led by former prime minister Nawaz Sharif. Perceived as pro-business, its main power base is in Sharif's populous home province of Punjab. The PML was last in power for 30 months to July 1993.

-- Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) was founded last year by Pakistan's former cricket captain Imran Khan. Fighting its first election, the fledgling party has made the fight against corruption the main plank of its platform.

-- Pakistan People's Party-Shaheed Bhutto (PPP-SB) was formed by Benazir's estranged brother Murtaza, who was killed in Karachi on September 20. His Lebanese-born widow Ghinwa now leads the party. Benazir's husband Asif Ali Zardari is in jail on a charge of conspiring to murder Murtaza. Zardari denies the charge.

-- Pakistan Muslim League-Junejo (PML-J) is led by former National Assembly speaker Hamid Nasir Chattha. The PML-J was an ally of Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) in the ousted federal and Punjab provincial governments.

-- Awami National Party (ANP) was founded by Abdul Ghaffar Khan and is now led by Ajmal Khattak. The ANP, based in North West Frontier Province, helped the PPP struggle against martial law in the 1980s, but the allies fell out after the PPP won the 1988 election. The ANP is now allied with the PML.

-- Mohajir National Movement (MQM), led by Altaf Hussain, is fighting for the rights of Urdu-speaking Mohajir Moslems who fled to Pakistan from India at partition in 1947. The MQM, strong in Karachi, boycotted the 1993 National Assembly election, but did well in the provincial assembly election.
-- MQM (Haqiqi) is a splinter group led by Afaq Ahmad which began operating in Karachi when the army launched a big security operation against the MQM in June 1992.

-- Jamaat-i-Islami, led by Qazi Hussain Ahmad, is Pakistan's biggest religious party and bitterly opposed to Bhutto. It is boycotting the elections on the grounds that corrupt politicians should be brought to book and barred from standing in the polls.

-- Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam (JUI-F) led by Maulana Fazalur Rehman, former chairman of the National Assembly's foreign affairs committee, is sympathetic to Afghanistan's Islamic Taleban militia. Its main support lies in North West Frontier Province. The party was an ally of the PPP during the last government.

-- Jamiat Ulema-i-Pakistan (JUI-S) is led by Maulana Samiul Haq, who broke with JUI-F after differences with Fazalur Rehman. JUI-S is close to the PML and Jamaat-i-Islami. Many Afghan Taleban members have studied in JUI-S religious schools.
-- Pakistan Democratic Party (PDP) is led by Nawabzada Nasrullah Khan, a veteran politician aligned with the PPP.

-- Tehrik-e-Jafria Pakistan (TJP), formed in 1992, is the political wing of the militant Shi'ite Moslem Tehrik-e-Nifaz Fiqah Jafria (TNFJ) group, founded in 1979. Its leader is Allama Syed Sajid Ali Naqvi. Inspired partly by the 1979 Islamic revolution in Iran, the TJP feuds with militant Sunni Moslems.

-- Sipah-e-Sahaba Pakistan (SSP) is a militant Sunni Moslem group founded in 1985 by a breakaway leader of Jamiat Ulema-i-Islam, Maulana Haq Nawaz Jehangvi, who was assassinated in 1990. His successor, Zia-ur-Rahman Faruqi, was killed in a bomb blast in Lahore in January. The SSP, bitterly opposed to Shi'ites, whom it regards as non-Moslems, is now led by Maulana Azam Tariq.
